name: At-home fractional laser
lead: An at-home fractional laser is a handheld, low-energy, typically non-ablative device that delivers light to the skin in a grid of tiny zones, leaving surrounding tissue untouched. Consumer versions are sold for fine lines, uneven texture and mild scarring on the face, and are lower-powered relatives of clinic fractional resurfacing.

The clinic technology has a substantial literature. Fractional photothermolysis with a 1,550 nm erbium fibre laser was studied for atrophic scars in 2007, a consensus report addressed ablative fractional resurfacing for traumatic scars in 2014, and systematic reviews have examined fractional CO2 lasers for depressed acne scars.[3][4][5] Home devices have a much thinner evidence base.

A 2026 review of home-based dermatologic devices for acne and rejuvenation and a 2022 systematic review of home-based dermatology devices are the main overviews; the latter included 37 studies of 16 devices, and found no double-blinded randomized trials among them.[1][2] The 2022 review's laser findings concerned hair growth in androgenic alopecia and not fractional skin resurfacing.[2]
infobox: Strong for clinic lasers; limited for home units

paras: Fractional lasers split the beam into many microscopic columns of thermal injury. Clinic devices are divided into ablative systems, such as CO2 lasers that vaporise tissue columns, and non-ablative systems, such as 1,550 nm erbium-doped fibre lasers, which heat without removing tissue.[3][5] Home devices use the non-ablative approach at much lower energy, so treatments are repeated over time. Reviews of energy-based devices in skin of colour note non-ablative fractional lasers target water rather than melanin, which is described as safer for darker skin types.[6]

The accepted model is that the microscopic injury columns trigger wound healing and new collagen production in the surrounding intact tissue, while the faster healing allows shorter recovery than fully ablative resurfacing. A 2011 editorial introduced fractional laser resurfacing in this way.[7]

In clinic settings, a 2022 meta-analysis of six articles with 467 patients found ultra-pulsed CO2 fractional laser scored higher for skin smoothness than comparator methods in depressed acne scars.[3] A 2007 study applied 1,550 nm fractional photothermolysis to atrophic scars.[5] A 2020 randomized split-face study and other trials examined combinations with exosomes, microneedling radiofrequency and poly-L-lactic acid.[8][9][10]

For home devices, a 2022 review of home-based dermatology devices found laser evidence mainly for hair regrowth and RF evidence for wrinkles, and concluded that home devices appeared safe and effective for several uses but that trials were few, unblinded or short.[2] A 2026 review of home-based devices for acne and rejuvenation is reported to rank fractional lasers, LED and radiofrequency among categories with the best balance of efficacy and safety; its abstract could not be examined in full.[1] No systematic review focused solely on home fractional lasers was identified.

A 2010 review of complications of fractionated laser resurfacing and a study of 961 treatments catalogue side effects of clinic procedures, which include erythema, edema, pigment change, infection and scarring in the professional setting.[11][12] Home devices deliver less energy and carry a lower expected risk, but misuse, unsuitable skin types and inadequate sun protection are recognised concerns in dermatology reviews.[6][11]

Clinic-based trials and meta-analyses of fractional lasers are extensive for acne scars, hypertrophic scars and melasma.[3][4][13] For home-use fractional lasers specifically, evidence is limited to broad reviews of home devices that did not isolate them.[1][2]
